text:
IFF Statement on the Information Technology (IGDME) Amendment Rules, 2026

The Government of India today notified the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026, concerning synthetically generated information (SGI). While these rules claim to address AI-generated content harms such as deepfakes, they introduce severe digital rights violations that fundamentally undermine constitutional protections and worsen problems that IFF had flagged in our November 2025 submissions on the draft rules.​

1. Accelerated Censorship Through Compressed Timelines The notified rules drastically compress content removal timelines, transforming intermediaries into rapid fire censors. Government takedown orders must now be complied with within three hours (reduced from 36 hours in the draft), while Grievance Appellate Committee orders must be actioned within two hours (down from 24 hours). User complaints on significant social media intermediaries must be resolved within seven days (reduced from 15 days), with urgent cases requiring action within 36 hours (down from 72 hours). These impossibly short timelines eliminate any meaningful human review, forcing platforms toward automated over-removal and creating a prior restraint regime incompatible with Article 19(1)(a). It is notable that in many of these censorship actions a copy of the notice or hearing is never provided to the person whose content is removed. Hence, the entire process is secretive and in violation of natural justice. 

2. Expansion of Prohibited Content Categories : The rules introduce sweeping new prohibitions absent from the draft that was put to consultation. Rule 3(3)(a)(i) now categorically bans SGI that "results in the creation, generation, modification or alteration of any false document or false electronic record". This vague formulation could criminalize legitimate uses of AI in document preparation, research outputs, and creative works. The rules also prohibit SGI "falsely depicting or portraying" persons or events "in a manner that is likely to deceive", language so broad it could capture satire, parody, political commentary, and artistic expression.​

3. Identity Disclosure to Private Parties : A particularly troubling addition is Rule 3(1)(ca)(ii)(III), which mandates disclosure of violating users' identities directly to complainants who claim to be victims. This bypasses judicial oversight and creates serious risks of harassment, doxing, and vigilante action, especially against marginalized users and dissenting voices.​ This is due to the absence of any anchoring language for the need to get a court order or an order pursuant to a criminal investigation. 

4. Continued Violation of Safe Harbor Framework: Despite IFF's submissions highlighting incompatibility with Section 79 of the IT Act and the Shreya Singhal precedent, the rules continue to impose proactive monitoring obligations that transform intermediaries from neutral conduits into active censors of speech. The requirement to "deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures" including "automated tools" to prevent uploads violating "any law for the time being in force" creates an impossible compliance burden across India's complex legal landscape.

The notified rules represent a regression from the already problematic draft that we had called to be withdrawn and instead approach AI based content risks beyond the existing safe harbor framework. We believe AI technologies do need to be regulated however deeply disagree with the approach of the Union Government that has over time expanded its censorship powers against the framework and rights under the Constitution of India. 

IFF will publish a detailed first-read analysis tomorrow examining the constitutional, technical, and human rights implications of these amendments.

Celebrating RTI Act on 12th October : Objective incomplete without Citizen’s Charter and Grievance Redressal Bill

There was a proposal to introduce “The Right of Citizens for Time Bound Delivery of Goods and Services and Redressal of their Grievances Bill, 2011” (The Citizen’s Charter and Grievance Redressal Bill) after implementation of “Right-To-Information Act, 2005” to fulfill the objective of providing timely redressal of Grievances to the public. But unfortunately the much-awaited and most desired bill has still not been introduced. Rather “The Citizen’s Charter and Grievance Redressal Bill” is much more necessary to achieve the desired goal. Union Government should fulfill the much-needed requirement by introducing the said bill which will make government-functionaries to solve problems of the people in an effective manner reducing over-burdened government-functionaries presently utilizing much of their time and resources Under Right-To-Information Act. Rather with quick disposal of public-grievances through “The Citizen’s Charter and Grievance Redressal Bill” will make government-functionaries working fast thus resulting in further savings of time and resources of government-departments and public authorities.

Otherwise also, a fresh look is necessary for revising RTI Rules drafted long back in the year 2012 to prevent misuse of RTI Act which will further drastically reduced time and resources of public authority spent on handling RTI matters. Ever since first amendment in RTI Act was done ever since its implementation on 12th October2005, some NGOs and opposition parties are crying that sunshine Act is diluted! But the amendment made in the year 2019 aimed to change status and tenure of Information Commissioners, in no way affected users of RTI Act. Insertion of section 44(3) in “The Digital Personal Data Protection Act 2023” removing riders to section 8(1)(j) of RTI Act in fact necessary to preserve Parliamentary privilege and remove confusion through the term “public-interest”. Having a rider of “Public Interest” was not needed in view of section 8(2) of RTI Act which provides access to information in case public interest overweighs the harm protected. It is for the first time that Central Information Commission has full strength of Chief Information Commissioner and ten Information Commissioners sworn on 15.12.2025.

Otherwise also, earlier two Commissioners went on disposing the cases at a fast speed with Vinod Kumar Tiwari having disposed of 12700 cases with quality judgements elaborately worded in a short span of just 24 months while this figure does not include matters of Show-Cause notices and Non-Compliance matters. It is significant that he even heard some cases on different dates to ensure enough opportunity to respondent public-authorities to defend their case like in his verdict dated 16.01.2025 in petition-number CIC/GNCTD/A/2024/108412 in the matter “Sanjeev Kumar versus Directorate of Health Services (GNCTD”. He even imposed penalty on the PIO and awarded compensation to the petitioner apart from making recommendations while highlighting malpractices in working of private hospitals with DHS being the mute spectator.  Even Delhi High Court dismissed a writ-petition WPC 596/2026 against this verdict on first day of hearing i.e. 16.01.2026. Even present Chief Information Commissioner Raj Kumar Goyal echoed likewise in his verdict dated 16.01.2026 observing that despite 20 years of implementation of the RTI Act, public information officers and first appellate authorities in DHS (GNCTD) were not alert to their legal responsibilities terming it to be a serious issue.

At the same time, Vinod Kumar Tiwari praised such officers who respond to matters nicely not only while responding to RTI applications, but also while presenting their case before the Commission. Example is decision dated 17.11.2025 in file-number CIC/DDATY/A/2024/114518 in the matter “Pawan Jindal versus Delhi Development Authority (DDA)” where he praised Rahul Gupta, PIO-cum-Executive Engineer (DDA) for his nicely presenting the case before the Commission.  Such praise in a CIC-verdict motivates others to do similar nice work to handle RTI matters.

However, RTI rules (and not the RTI Act) need important modifications mainly to prevent misuse of the Act and minimising challenge to CIC verdicts in courts. Notification should be to declare all public-private-partnerships, sports-bodies, cooperative-societies and other such bodies, public-authorities under RTI Act. Land and Building Departments of central and state governments should study all cases of allotment of land or government-accommodations at subsidised rates or lease, and declare all these as public-authorities under RTI Act. For future, land or government-accommodations should be provided at subsidised rates on pre-condition of beneficiaries coming under purview of RTI Act.

Offices like those of President, Prime Minister, Governor, Lt Governor and Chief Minister must not act like “Post Offices” by transferring RTI applications under section 6(3) of RTI Act to concerned departments. These offices should entertain RTI applications pertaining to their respective offices only, and returning rest others to RTI applicants advising applicants to file RTI applications directly to concerned departments.

Considering vast participation of public-money in private sector banks, all private sector banks must be under purview of RTI Act. Already all employees up-to highest post of CMD are public servants according to Banking Regulation Act. Reserve Bank of India (RBI) had to impose restrictions on withdrawal of money for some time on a prominent private sector bank. Former CMD of another prominent private sector Bank is under arrest for serious charges of misappropriation of public-money in the Bank. Inspection Reports of private banks revealed under RTI Act by RBI reveal gross misuse of public money by top management. Another private sector bank is in notoriety for large number of Non-Performing Assets (NPAs). Heavy fluctuation in share-prices of certain private sector banks tend to doubt regarding safety of public money in private sector banks. Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (RBI subsidiary) has to pay maximum rupees five lakhs from state-funds to each depositor of the bank including those in private sector which collapses due to massive irregularities, which is public-funding to declare private sector banks as “public-authorities” under section 2(h) of RTI Act.

Section 27 and 28 of RTI Act give power to Competent Authorities and state-governments to draft their own rules which include fixing of RTI fees. Several Competent Authorities and states misused their power by having RTI fees as high as rupees 500However Supreme Court in its verdict dated 20.03.2018 imposed a capping of rupees fifty to be maximum RTI fees. RTI-fees should be uniformly rupees 50 inclusive of copying-charges of first twenty copied pages Making basic RTI-fees at rupees fifty will largely prevent misuse of RTI Act. There must not be any fees for filing First or Second Appeals.

Handling cost of a postal-order of value rupees ten costs postal-department about rupees fifty with cost of handling of postal-orders by a public-authority and bank-clearing even extra. Postal Department should issue special RTI-stamps (like earlier stamps for licence-fees of radios and TV sets) in denominations of rupees 2, 10 and 50 which will save crores of rupees annually to public-exchequers in using postal-orders as mode of payment of RTI fees.  These RTI stamps should be available at all post-offices and counters of public-authorities and other convenient sale-points. Post-free RTI-applications addressed to central public-authorities should be accepted at all about 160000 post-offices rather than just about 4500 post offices presently. It is not difficult because every post-office however small it may be, daily sends post-bag to Head Post Office with registered post, cash and unsold revenue-articles. This post-bag can carry post-free RTI-applications received at the post-office.

Decision dated 02.11.2012 by Punjab & Haryana High Court in the matter “Fruit and Vegetable Union versus Unknown” (CWP 4787 of 2011) requiring ID proof compulsorily with every RTI application, First Appeal and petitions filed with Information Commissions should be compulsorily adopted throughout the country Police-enquiry conducted at behest of some Indian missions abroad established that a petitioner approached Central Information Commission with name and address both of which did not exist. RTI-responses and orders of First Appellate Authorities should be auto-emailed rather than RTI-applicants required to search portals for viewing of RTI-responses and orders by First Appellate Authorities. Websites designed by National Informatics Centre (NIC) for central public-authorities should be mandatorily for all states. This has become necessary for state like Odisha which has made online filing of RTI-applications a mockery when it is compulsory to download online-filled RTI-application, and then send it by post to concerned department.

Delhi High Court in its order dated 08.08.2018 in WPC 8278 of 2018 in the matter “Anil Dutt Sharma versus Government of NCT Delhi and others” mentioned – This Court is of the prima facie view that the Right-To-Information Act, 2005 would now override the Delhi Right To Information Act, 2001. DRTI Act has lost all with implementation of RTI Act 2005. Very few applications are filed under DRTI Act. All such acts legislated by individual states, before RTI Act 2005 came into existence must be repealed.

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

Statement: MeitY’s “enhanced diligence” advisory pressures platforms to police protest speech. It must be withdrawn.

October 9, 2026

On October 8, MeitY’s Cyber Laws Division sent an advisory to all social media intermediaries. It asks them to exercise “enhanced diligence” over false, misleading, manipulated or out-of-context content linked to “ongoing public events and developments”, to “identify, prevent and not promote” unlawful information, to label or “contextualise” misleading content, and to prioritise complaints from “authorised Government agencies” on public-order content. It takes effect immediately. MeitY has not published it and its text became public through MediaNama. It was issued as citizens protest in Delhi and Mumbai over the revision of electoral rolls, with a protest called at Jantar Mantar for October 10. We call on MEITY to withdraw it.

First, the advisory names no provision that empowers MeitY to issue it and such advisories are not issued under any law. Section 79(2)(c) of the IT Act conditions safe harbour on “due diligence” and on guidelines the Central Government may “prescribe”, that is, by rules notified and laid before Parliament under Section 87. The IT Rules recognise only “due diligence” under Rule 3 and “additional due diligence” for significant social media intermediaries under Rule 4. The phrase, “Enhanced diligence” used in this Advisory appears in neither. Further, MeitY’s proposed Rule 3(4) in the last round of Amendments mooted to the IT Rules, 2021, which has not been notified further confirms this does not have any legal character. Second, an advisory cannot alter the application of existing law. Rule 3(1)(b)(v) covers only misinformation communicated “knowingly and intentionally” that is “patently false and untrue or misleading in nature”. The advisory drops both qualifiers and adds “social tranquility”, neither that nor “misleading” is a ground for restricting speech under Article 19(2).

Third, facing an undefined standard platforms will censor more than the law requires. The advisory asks them to “identify, prevent and not promote” unlawful information and to “strengthen their existing monitoring”. This is proactive monitoring by another name, which the Rules contemplate only for narrow categories such as child sexual abuse material. Further, it is vague and does does not define “authorised Government agencies” or “priority”, and does not require platforms to tell users that a government complaint lay behind an action. Users will see only a platform decision. The State’s role disappears, and with it any route to challenge that role in court. The advisory governs public speech but is not itself public. It cites no statutory provision, is approved by an unnamed “competent authority”, and does not identify the events or content that prompted it.

We anticipate a huge spike in censorship over the next few days.

We call on MeitY to:
1. Publish the advisory in full, including any clause (v), and state the provision under which it was issued.
2. Withdraw it, or clarify that it creates no obligations beyond the IT Act and Rules and that “enhanced diligence” is not a condition of safe harbour.
3. Disclose which agencies are sending complaints under it, and how many.
4. Abandon the proposed Rule 3(4).

We also call on platforms to:
1. Disclose all government complaints and requests received under this advisory.
2. Act only on requests that meet the Shreya Singhal standard and Rule 3(1)(d).
3. Refrain from proactively filtering or downranking protest content on the basis of this advisory.
4. Notify affected users, including when an action follows a government complaint.

Last week the US Justice Department charged two men over an alleged scheme to sell counterfeit Ozempic from China to US distributors.

US law requires a unique serial number on every package of a prescription drug. The counterfeit cartons carried false serial numbers, and one of them, 430834149057, is on every unit in the shipments it lists: about 47 units in September 2023, 924 in November, and 1,008 ten days later.

This is a very well established pattern for counterfeiters: put something plausible on the packaging, no-one will have the time to actually check it.

This time though.. someone did! In fact on 19 November 2023 an alleged co-conspirator warned that every unit had the same serial number, and that a trading partner who noticed would have to quarantine it and report it to the FDA. 

In December the FDA published that exact serial number in a public warning. A contact at one of the buyers asked whether the warning would affect a pending order for 60,000 more units. and of course one of the two men charged, replied: "Not at all."

A public warning only covers the serial number the FDA has already found, and the next batch can carry a different one. The cloned serial only flares red when someone compares serial numbers across cartons and deliveries. So the practical question is: would the receiving process of warehouses/distributors flag the anomaly? Apparently very few do because it takes a lot of time.

Btw, this is exactly one of the use cases for EUIPO Authentic View standard and one of the reasons why I started Eonpass: you have to dig into the supply chain to understand what's happening, looking at labels is one of the many steps in an investigation.

IFF's statement on the AI Impact Summit 2026.

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) welcomes the India AI Impact Summit 2026 (February 16-20) as an important platform for global dialogue on, "Artificial Intelligence". We believe the Summit's agenda and framing fundamentally misalign with the lived reality of AI deployment in India, an environment marked by rising digital authoritarianism and the systematic erosion of constitutional protections that are causing demonstrable harm to vulnerable populations. Its official framing centers on “People, Planet and Progress”, with Prime Minister Narendra Modi inaugurating and world leaders like France’s President Emmanuel Macron and top tech CEOs (Google’s Sundar Pichai, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, etc.) expected to attend. The Summit's optimistic narrative about AI for development obscures the reality of how its deployment is impacting people in their everyday lives.

The current environment is one of a sharp contraction in civic space, where recent governance proposals on technology have facilitated the expansion of state power that run contrary to the state commitments on fundamental rights and social justice. Today, there exists few organisations in India that work on digital rights and those which are surviving are severely under resourced, suffer from burdensome compliances, growing legal risks and deliberate exclusion from policy making processes. The decline of civil society work is matching the growth of private and public sector capacity to lobby the policy making processes. So, even before a question is prompted, how should Indian civil society engage with the India AI Impact Summit, a predicate and grounded inquiry is, how many independent, Indian civil society groups exist in India that have capacity and can be critical of state policies and practices around AI?

In the recent past, far from fostering accountability, India’s digitisation drive is often used to sidestep constitutional safeguards of transparency, harming communities and individuals. For instance, recent legal changes have weakened the Right to Information (RTI) framework, curtailing citizens’ ability to question power. The Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 introduced an amendment (Section 8(1)(j) to the RTI Act) that blocks access to any information labeled “personal information”, allowing officials to deny critical information. Likewise, digitisation of welfare governance has been weaponized to bypass accountability, with digitisation often becoming a gatekeeper and working to the detriment of the poor. A stark development came in December, 2025 when Parliament hastily passed the Viksit Bharat - Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 (VB-GRAM G), repealing the landmark MGNREGA jobs guarantee program. VB-GRAM G converted a demand driven legal right to work into a discretionary, bureaucratically controlled scheme, undermining decades of workers’ rights. There are references to "AI" within the text of the objects and reasons that are a part of this law.

Beyond this, India's policies on AI also demonstrate a wider embrace of de-regulation narratives to ensure, "innovation". For instance, the Union Budget 2026 unveiled a 20-year tax holiday (until 2047) for foreign firms using Indian data centers, aiming to lure global AI infrastructure. Yet, this policy was formulated with scant regard for its impact on local communities and natural resources. Other recent measures also deserve comment:

Sanchar Saathi : In late 2025, the government ordered smartphone manufacturers to pre-install a government cybersecurity application called Sanchar Saathi on all devices. The app was ostensibly meant to secure citizens’ phones, but the mandatory installation sparked outrage over privacy and surveillance concerns, drawing parallels to spyware abuse.
The ‘Sahyog’ Censorship Portal: In 2024, the Union Home Ministry quietly launched the Sahyog Portal to expedite content-blocking orders on social media and websites. Under this system, law enforcement agencies can flag “unlawful” online content and directly trigger its takedown by internet platforms, all through a centralized interface.
Expansion of NATGRID: Perhaps the most far-reaching is the quiet expansion of NATGRID, India’s National Intelligence Grid. Long conceived as an integrated database for counter-terror investigations, NATGRID has recently morphed into a broad surveillance net. Following a high-level police conference in late November 2025, states were directed to “scale up” NATGRID usage beyond central agencies, even giving police officers at the Superintendent rank access to its vast datasets.
These developments match the increased use of AI technologies in domains of policing and welfare without a clear legal basis and real safeguards.

IFF acknowledges that the India AI Impact Summit 2026 offers a platform for dialogue and a chance for civil society voices to gain visibility on an international stage. We recognize the value in having digital rights perspectives included in global AI governance conversations, indeed, the Summit’s presence in India is an opportunity to spotlight our constitutional concerns before a world audience. We support our peer organizations and allies who choose to engage with the Summit, and we will remain in constructive collaboration with them. However, IFF has decided not to allocate significant organizational resources to direct participation in the Summit’s events. This is not a boycott of the forum, but a practical choice of focus. As a small team of only 7 full-time staff based in New Delhi, we must prioritize the most pressing advocacy initiatives that align closely with our mission and charter.

This includes ongoing efforts such as legal challenges to unconstitutional regulations, campaigning and community engagement for strengthening free expression, privacy and transparency frameworks. These are battles immediately affecting citizens’ rights and requiring our sustained attention. IFF will engage with the Summit in a mindful, critical manner. We will track the proceedings and outcomes closely, offering our analyses and critiques rooted in constitutional values. If and where we do participate (for example, in side events or discussions), we will do so with a critical gaze, centering the lived experiences of Indians and the paramountcy of our fundamental rights. Our support is firmly with the broader civil society coalition pushing for AI governance that is accountable and just.

DEMOCRACY CANNOT BE PROTECTED BY SILENCING VOTERS

Rejinagar demands independent scrutiny—not blind political loyalty.

During the October 6 West Bengal bypoll, serious allegations were raised about voter intimidation, removal/detention of opposition polling agents and police interference. More significantly, Scroll reported that its journalists personally witnessed Muslim voters being turned away from a polling station in Rejinagar. The report also documented allegations that opposition agents were prevented from functioning and that local journalists' social-media pages were restricted before polling. 

Humayun Kabir was also detained by police during polling after a confrontation; Indian Express, India Today and The Economic Times independently reported the detention. 

At the same time, the Election Commission's general observer, Harshal Pancholi, told Scroll that he considered the poll free and fair after examining video evidence. That makes the demand for transparent, booth-level verification of the competing claims even more important. 

So the resistance must ask precise questions:

- Which voters were prevented from voting?
- At which booths?
- Were their names on the electoral roll?
- Why were opposition polling agents removed or detained?
- What did CCTV/webcasting footage show?
- Why were journalists' pages restricted immediately before polling?
- Were complaints independently investigated?
- Will the Election Commission publish the relevant evidence and its findings?
- If irregularities are established, will affected booths be repolled?

No citizen should lose the right to vote because of religion, political affiliation or administrative intimidation.

And no constitutional institution should demand faith instead of evidence.

DO NOT ASK PEOPLE TO “TRUST” ANY SIDE.
ASK FOR THE EVIDENCE.
PROTECT EVERY ELIGIBLE VOTER.
PROTECT EVERY LAWFUL POLLING AGENT.
PROTECT INDEPENDENT JOURNALISM.
PROTECT THE VERIFIABILITY OF THE VOTE.

If the allegations are false, an independent investigation should establish that clearly.

If they are true, accountability and corrective action must follow.

That is not partisan politics.

THAT IS DEMOCRATIC ACCOUNTABILITY.

Independent reporting to circulate:

- [Scroll — Ground report on Rejinagar polling]
 (https://t.co/9xe51YjFBR)
- [Alt News — Restrictions on local journalists' Facebook pages]
 (https://t.co/8n00IRSu4C)
- [Indian Express — Humayun Kabir detained during Rejinagar voting]
 (https://t.co/cRxykbr23E)
- [India Today — Video of Kabir's detention and allegations of polling interference]
 (https://t.co/CcXOCFFzZ8)
- [Times of India — Allegations of police interference and demand for fresh polling]
 (https://t.co/YRVPdiJd8o)

The strongest resistance is not “believe our side.” It is: SHOW THE EVIDENCE, AUDIT THE PROCESS, PROTECT THE VOTE.

#WATCH | Hyderabad, Telangana: On the CEC row, BRS  MP Vaddiraju Ravichandra says, "...In the states, out of 3.5 crore voters, 1 crore are being removed; did 1 crore voters all die? Did they just vanish? What kind of system is this? They are working to ensure the BJP comes to power in future elections; they are strategising to defeat specific MLAs and ensure a BJP victory. This is wrong... Even though there are three commissioners on the panel, the other two have repeatedly—on fourteen occasions over ten months—objected, stating that certain decisions were flawed. He listens to no one—neither the public nor political leaders..."

On 10 October, before the next march, remember who wanted this cleanup.
In June 2018 a Congress delegation led by Kamal Nath handed the Election Commission a memorandum. Their charge: about 60 lakh duplicate, illegal and false voters in Madhya Pradesh, and that the BJP government in the state had put them on the roll. Sachin Pilot made the same charge in Rajasthan, about 41 lakh. They went to the Supreme Court because, by their account, the Commission was not deleting fast enough. The Commission told the Court it had already removed about 24 lakh entries between January and July 2018, later put near 29 lakh. On 12 October 2018 the Court dismissed both petitions.
So in 2018, according to them, the illegal voter was a BJP voter, and deletion was democracy.
In 2026 the same leaders are on the street because names have been deleted under the Special Intensive Revision.
 Now, according to them, the deleted voter is their voter, and deletion is vote chori.
Resign, Gyanesh Kumar. Scrap the revision. Put the names back.

The roll did not change its character. Their interest in it did.

When the fake entry was supposedly voting for the other side, they dragged the Commission to court to delete it.
When the cleanup reaches names they now claim as their own, the same deletion is an attack on democracy. A dead voter, a shifted voter and a duplicate entry do not have a party. A convenient list does.

SIR generated disenfranchisement of millions, Election Commission of India’s unilateral modification of Form 6 admittedly under the cover of approval of Supreme Court which denies having given any such approval and grossly inadequate measures to deal with the fate of deleted voters has fatally imperilled democracy. The restoration of deleted voters in electoral roll, if at all done by a compromised ECI, has meant, in Mahatma Gandhi’s words, “sending a reprieve after hanging”

https://t.co/UooTJDXlO8

FIRST THE FORM CHANGED. NOW THE COURSE IS BEING CORRECTED.
SO WHO WILL ANSWER THE QUESTIONS?

A voter registration form should make democracy more accessible—not more complicated.

The controversy around Form 6 during the SIR exercise is therefore not a minor technical dispute.

The Indian Express reported that a new declaration was added to Form 6 on the ECI's online portal, requiring applicants to provide information concerning their own or their parents' or grandparents' presence in earlier electoral rolls. Two Election Commissioners reportedly objected to the change, describing it as unauthorised and calling for its removal.

The Election Commission has disputed the suggestion of an institutional split, saying differing views are part of its decision-making process and that its decisions were ultimately unanimous.

But then comes a development that deserves attention.

On September 29, the ECI directed states where SIR had been completed to identify eligible voters who were left out of the rolls and facilitate their enrolment through Form 6. Booth Level Officers were instructed to compare pre-SIR and post-SIR rolls and identify people whose names had disappeared.

That is not a trivial administrative detail.

It raises a fundamental democratic question:

If a voter was legitimately entitled to be on the electoral roll, how did that voter get left out in the first place?

And another:

Who is responsible for detecting and correcting the error?

The answer cannot be political rhetoric from either side.

It must be records, procedures, audit trails, explanations and accountability.

A democratic election requires more than polling day.

It requires a trustworthy chain:

Registration → Electoral Roll → Verification → Correction → Voting → Counting.

If any link in that chain becomes opaque, citizens have every legitimate reason to demand answers.

The issue is not about protecting one institution from criticism.

It is about protecting the credibility of the institution that protects the citizen's vote.

The Election Commission can withstand scrutiny.

Indeed, a constitutional institution should welcome scrutiny.

Because democracy does not become weaker when citizens ask difficult questions.

Democracy becomes weaker when questions are treated as disloyalty.

The simplest democratic principle is also the most powerful:

Every eligible citizen deserves a fair opportunity to register, remain on the electoral roll and exercise the right to vote.

And when mistakes occur—

correct them, explain them, document them, and make sure they cannot quietly happen again.

India has expunged 130 million names from its electoral register over the preceding twelve months. Approximately 130 million citizens participated in the most recent national election. According to the Election Commission, the removal process targets deceased individuals, duplicate registrations, and ineligible voters. However, the chief's two deputies have raised objections on at least 14 occasions within a 10-month period. A youth-led movement has subsequently mobilised public demonstrations calling for the chief's resignation.

The  Mass Disenfranchisement Of Indians (MODI) through the Shah Instigated Removal (SIR) is shrinking India’s electorate. 

According to an analysis published in a leading business daily, the SIR has reduced the size of the Indian electorate to its 2015 level. The electorate across 31 states and UTs grew from 81.7 Cr in 2015 to about 95 Cr before the SIR process began. But the SIR has brought it down to 81.8 Cr. This reversal is unprecedented.

This has been done through a mass deletion of over 13 crore voters during the SIR’s draft roll stage. The actual number of deletions is even higher, and the electorate will shrink further as SIR is still ongoing in 14 states and UTs.

In Maharashtra, the data reveals the Vote Chori pattern: first, the electorate grew by 5.6% between the 2024 Lok Sabha election and the SIR. Now, the SIR has shrunk it by 21%. The disastrous Delhi SIR has shrunk the electorate by 16% compared to its 2014 level.

The capture of our electoral system by the RSS-BJP through the Election Commission of India cannot be allowed to stand. We will ensure that every voter that has been illegitimately removed is restored to the electoral roll.

🇮🇳|October 4, 2026, Mumbai. Thousands took to the streets, marching from Metro Cinema to the headquarters of the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation. Dubbed the "Virat Garjana Morcha" (Grand Roar Rally), the protest was jointly led by Shiv Sena (UBT) leader Uddhav Thackeray and MNS leader Raj Thackeray.

The stated demands were clear: the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, the cancellation of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) in Maharashtra, and a return to paper ballots. Uddhav labeled Kumar a "weapon of the BJP," while Raj shouted, "Gyanesh *kaka* [Uncle Gyanesh], don't steal votes."

Yet, this was merely the tip of the iceberg. The protest revealed far more than a dispute over electoral procedures; it exposed a functioning, systematic mechanism aimed not at "cleaning up the rolls," but at reshaping the voter demographic to favor the ruling party.

💀 The First Layer of Truth: The 20.7 Million Deleted Voters Were No "Mistake"

When the draft electoral roll for Maharashtra's SIR was released on August 31, 2026, 20,688,487 voters were left off the list representing 21.14% of the state's 97.9 million voters.

However, this figure itself is misleading. Data analysis by *The Hindu* revealed a pattern of "blatantly arbitrary and capricious deletions."  

Key Data:

◾ In 58 constituencies, at least one-third of the voters were removed. Among these, 25 constituencies saw a removal rate of 40% or higher. Almost all these constituencies are concentrated in Mumbai, Pune, Thane, and Nashik urban areas that have historically leaned towards the opposition.
◾Bhiwandi East in Thane recorded a removal rate of 49.1%; out of 376,000 voters, 185,000 were removed.
◾"Permanent migration" and "untraceable or absent" were used as catch-all categories for removal. In Kalyan Rural, out of 252,000 removals, 239,000 (96.5%) were labeled as "migrated or absent," whereas only 4,882 cases of death were recorded in the same constituency.
◾Across 85 constituencies, "migration" and "absence" accounted for between 75% and 96.5% of all removals. These 85 constituencies had a combined voter base of 32.1 million prior to the Special Intensive Revision (SIR); 11.7 million (36.3%) were removed. Of these removals, 9.79 million (84%) were categorized as "migrated or absent."

However, the Election Commission's own manual stipulates that absent voters cannot be removed, as they remain ordinary residents of the area. An Election Commission FAQ also states that "absent" means the "elector could not be contacted." Analysis reveals that these two grounds were used arbitrarily and interchangeably across multiple constituencies.

This is not "data cleaning." This is organized removal.

🎯 The Second Layer of Truth: Who was removed? Muslims, Dalits, and migrants.

If the SIR was merely about "purging the deceased and migrants," why was the pattern of removal so systematically concentrated in specific communities?

The data does not lie:

◾In 38 constituencies where the Muslim population exceeds 20%, 29.77% of voters were labeled as "untraceable."  This means nearly 30% of voters vanished from the rolls overnight.
◾In constituencies with the largest Muslim populations, the deletion rate soared to 49%.
◾Deletion rates among Dalits and tribal communities were also higher than the state average. In the 29 constituencies reserved for Scheduled Castes, the average deletion rate was 19.6%; while slightly lower than the 30% seen in Muslim constituencies, it remains significant.
◾The Congress party has stated that these deletions disproportionately affect economically and socially marginalized groups, claiming that in most major states, more women than men were removed from the rolls.

When 30% to 49% of voters in Muslim constituencies are "deleted" while deletion rates in rural and upper-caste constituencies within the same state remain far lower that is not a "technical error." That is a targeted purge.

🔥 Truth Layer 3: Someone within the Election Commission is trying to stop this

Two of the three commissioners on the Election Commission of India formally recorded their objections.

Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi formally dissented on at least 14 occasions regarding decisions related to voter rolls, voter registration, and the Commission's technical systems.

In an internal memo, Sandhu explicitly stated that the Election Commission had acted against the written recommendations of the two commissioners, describing the actions as "unauthorized and illegal."

However, Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar disregarded these objections.

The Election Commission subsequently issued a clarification stating that all major decisions regarding the SIR (System for Integrated Registration) were unanimously approved by Kumar, claiming that reports of internal dissent did not amount to "institutional disagreement."

In simple language: two commissioners objected 14 times, yet the Chief Commissioner insisted, "We are unanimous."

That is not "unanimity." That is suppression.

🏛️ Truth Layer 4: The BJP’s "Electoral Genocide"

These are not my words. They are the words of actor and activist Prakash Raj.  On October 4, 2026, Raj stated in *The Hindu*:

“The BJP is using the Election Commission’s systematic, intensive revision process as a tool for electoral genocide. It has deleted 13 crore [130 million] voters, effectively declaring them non-citizens in their own country. This must be opposed until the entire process is scrapped and all voters' names are restored.”

13 crore. Nationwide.

On October 1, Congress leader Rahul Gandhi directly accused Prime Minister Modi, Home Minister Amit Shah, and Chief Election Commissioner Janesh Kumar of “destroying democracy” and committing “treason.”

Karnataka Deputy Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar accused BJP and JD(S) workers of submitting pre-filled Form 7s in bulk with the intent of deleting voters' names. The police have registered a case.

Congress’s Jairam Ramesh pointed out that in West Bengal, 91% of the names deleted during the Systematic Voters' Education and Electoral Participation (SVEEP) / Intensive Revision (SIR) process were restored after appeals meaning nearly nine out of ten deletions were erroneous.

🎭 The Fifth Layer of Truth: Who are the protest organizers?

The protest in Mumbai was not “spontaneous.”

On October 2, a youth organization named the “Cockroach Janta Party” (CJP) launched a “Jail Bharo Andolan” (Fill the Jails Movement) at Shivaji Park, demanding the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner. Despite the police denying permission, thousands of young people gathered at Shivaji Park.

The CJP had previously forced Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign. Now, they have set their sights on the Election Commission.

It is no coincidence that the Thackeray brothers launched their own “Great Roar Rally” two days after the CJP protest. This represents an attempt by the opposition to incorporate street protests into their own political agenda.  Yet, the CJP’s base of mobilization young people, civil society organizations, and the genuine voters whose names were purged by the SIR lies closer to the heart of this movement than any political party.

⚠️ The bottom line: This is not about the election itself. It is about who is permitted to vote.

The protests in Mumbai are not about "vote theft"; they are an act of resistance against "voter purging."

The SIR is not merely a "revision of electoral rolls." It is a political machine designed to delete voters who do not support the ruling party Muslims, Dalits, migrants, and the urban poor.

20.7 million voters were purged. In 38 Muslim-majority constituencies, 30% of the electorate was removed. In 58 constituencies, at least one-third of voters were deleted. 96.5% of these deletions were categorized as "migrated or absent" grounds that the Election Commission’s own manual explicitly states cannot justify a deletion.

Two Election Commissioners raised objections on 14 separate occasions, yet the Chief Commissioner overruled them. The Commission maintained a facade of unanimity.

This is not a "technical issue." It is a matter of democratic survival.

When a nation begins to systematically purge voters not because they have died or relocated, but because they do not belong to the "right" community, the "right" class, or the "right" political party, it ceases to be a democracy.

And the people on the streets of Mumbai are fighting against precisely that.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

New Delhi, 16 June 2026.

text:
Bitchat, the messaging app made by Twitter co-founder Jack Dorsey, has been removed from app stores in India.

Bitchat does not need the internet or a mobile network. Phones close to each other pass messages along over Bluetooth, so it keeps working even during an internet shutdown. Messages are encrypted and there is no central server.

The IT ministry ordered the removal on 3 October under Section 69A of the IT Act, the law the government uses to block websites and apps. The app is gone from Apple's App Store and Google Play in India, and its website does not open on many Indian internet providers.

In July, authorities had already asked GitHub to take down its code. The reason given then was that police cannot easily intercept or trace messages on it, and that it works during shutdowns.

India made up about 85% of all Bitchat downloads in one week of July, up from about 1% the month before.

The Internet Freedom Foundation, a digital rights group, says the law allows blocking unlawful content, not blocking an app because it works during shutdowns.

text:
Mahatma Gandhi once said that if this country is to progress in the right direction and to prevent its democracy from becoming the democracy of goons, young people must go to the villages and live there to serve.

After independence, people from Gandhian, Sarvodaya, progressive, and leftist ideologies have gone to villages to do service work.

These people work to organize villagers, remove superstitions, make them aware of their rights, and help with agriculture, health, and education.

In the village of Shukravaasa, Parvatpura Panchayat, in Dewas district of Madhya Pradesh, a group of young men and women are living in the village, making people aware and organized.

Among these youths are engineers, doctors, journalists, and filmmakers.

Because these young people are spreading awareness about democracy, the Constitution, and related matters, tribal people associated with their committee have started contesting elections for the Panchayat and Legislative Assembly.

This has angered the local people in power and political parties.

A short while ago, the police misbehaved with and assaulted these youths.

When these young people tried to hold a press conference against the attack, members of the Bajrang Dal—right in the presence of police and media—again assaulted them and stopped the press conference from happening.

An FIR was filed against their colleague Saurabh Banerjee for religious conversion, and he was illegally kept in police custody for 2 days. After that, he was kept in police remand for 7 more days, and then, without any evidence, he was sent to jail.

The most alarming thing this time is that the police filed an FIR against them for religious conversion.

Bajrang Dal’s allegation is that these people are making tribals into atheists.

If you read the FIR, the allegation is:

> “I greeted Saurabh by saying Ram Ram and asked what work he had. Saurabh replied, ‘What is this Ram Ram? Ram and Sita were brother and sister; they are not gods.’ Pressuring me, he said, ‘Hindu gods and goddesses are made of stone; what will happen by worshiping stone? God doesn’t exist at all, and you too should stop believing in God.’
After hearing this, I drove him out of my house. Saurabh has also made such provocative statements against Hindu gods and goddesses to other villagers before. Today, I told my father, Kamal Singh, about this, and he called other villagers—Nilesh Patel, Ravi Rawat, Manoj Patel, Brahmanand Chaudhary, Sunil Meena, and Vikas Parihar—and explained everything. Everyone suggested going to the police station to file a report.
Saurabh Banerjee has hurt our religious sentiments. Kindly register an FIR against Saurabh Banerjee.
Signature in Hindi: Petitioner Sachin, son of Kamal Singh Bamaniya, Village Shukravaasa, District Dewas, Date: 26.07.2025.”

According to Section 299 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, the anti-conversion law applies when you force someone to change from one religion to another through inducement or fear.

First of all, in the Indian Constitution, atheism is not a religion.

So, the anti-conversion law cannot even apply.

In India, there are millions of people like us who are atheists, and every day we consider atheism a scientific understanding. We try to tell everyone that God is an imagination, God cannot solve your problems—you must struggle yourself.

Will the Bajrang Dal tomorrow break into our homes, beat us, file FIRs against us, and make atheism a crime in this country?

Are we becoming a Hindu Taliban, where a blasphemy law is implemented, and under its name, speaking about superstition, blind faith, and promoting scientific thinking is declared a crime?

In Madhya Pradesh, the youth had set up a center for their organization, which the Madhya Pradesh government has now demolished with a bulldozer.

Tribals have come before the media and said that these people have never converted anyone’s religion.

But the Bajrang Dal and the police are intimidating the tribals and fabricating false cases against these young social workers.

If the police were to read the 22 vows of Babasaheb Ambedkar—the architect of our Constitution—they would put him in jail too, because in them Babasaheb made people pledge not to believe in Hindu gods and goddesses.

- Himanshu Kumar

#Bhojshala: Maa Vaghdevi's Temple or Kamal Maula Mosque 

On July 2, 2024, the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) was expected to submit its report on the ongoing survey at the complex, which serves as a temple on Tuesdays, a mosque on Fridays, and a tourist spot for the rest of the week. 

The survey, which has been ongoing for 98 days, has unearthed over 1710 relics and 39 idols of Hindu gods and goddesses, prompting the ASI to seek an extension from the court.

I visited the site on March 7, 2024, just before the court allowed the ASI team to conduct the survey. The entrance to the complex was marked by a police chowki, a board displaying directions, a chadar wala shop, and a ticket that read "Bhojshala and Kamal Maula Mosque."

A local activist associated with the struggle joined me and showed me the carvings inside the structure, the murtis unearthed during the 1952 survey, and a temporary structure constructed by Muslims at the Garbha Griha, which Hindus believe is the temple's sanctum sanctorum. 

The history of the site is marred by Islamic attacks, political unwillingness, and violence.

Outside the temple, surrounded by mosque-like structures and a Kamal Maula dargah, stands a Sankalp Jyoti mandir with an akhand jyoti. Hindus vow to keep this Jyoti burning with a Sankalp that they will not let it die until Maa Vaghdevi returns to her temple.

During my visit, everyone left their shoes outside, but two Muslims entered the complex with their shoes on, ignoring my request to remove them. The guard asked me to let them go. 

But the same people removed their shoes when they visited the structure referred to as Kamal Maula dargah situated next to Bhojshala complex. 

I hope to visit the complex again, this time with a changed scenario.

Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

I have my twitter back. 

It took me 6 days, a cyber police complaint and a legal notice to twitter to recover my account. 

If you got a DM from me last week asking you to vote for me for a podcast, that was not me. Please don't click it & If you already did, please change your password ASAP.

Here's what happened:

→I received a late night DM from a friend to vote on a podcast which redirected me to a a login page that looked right, and I typed in my password (classic)

→The attacker logged in and changed my 2FA within minutes & I was locked out of my account. (I still don't understand how my email and phone number were changed. Neither my email nor my phone was compromised.)

→Then he used account to DM followers a fake "vote for me" link. Each person who clicks becomes the next account sending it. That is how these spread.

What didn't work:

→ I filed X's hacked account form within the hour. Less than two hours later, the reply came: X could not verify me as the account owner. Their suggestion was to create a new account. Once 2FA is changed, the automated system treats the attacker as the real owner.

→ So I went to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, 2021, X must appoint a Resident Grievance Officer in India. He has no email address. X does not accept legal notices by email. 

The only options are a web form or post to their physical office.

Here's what worked:

→First, a cyber complaint on https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW (or call 1930).

→Second, a legal notice to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, impersonation complaints must be acted on within 24 hours.

→Third, the same notice sent by registered post, and to every X email address I could find.

The notice put X on record. It set out the ticket number, the phishing link, and the cyber complaint number. It showed proof of ownership: the registered email, the phone number, and the Premium subscription paid from my card. It ended with a clear ask and a deadline.

Six days after the hack, I was back in.

If this happens to you:
• Act within hours
• File X's hacked account form from your registered email and be persistent (this is important)
• File at https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW and keep the acknowledgement
• Notice to the Grievance Officer via the https://t.co/YkDfcMQwzE form and by post

Statement: IFF condemns the internet shutdown in Connaught Place ahead of today's protest. We are tracing the suspension order.

New Delhi, 2 October 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services in and around Connaught Place, New Delhi, this morning. At 9:40 am, Jio subscribers in the area received a message stating: "As per government instructions Internet services have been stopped in your area till further notice." The shutdown took effect before a protest called for 11 am at Jantar Mantar, seeking the resignation of the Chief Election Commissioner, had even begun. 

Delhi Police has refused permission for the gathering, prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 are in force across New Delhi district, and entry and exit at eleven metro stations have been closed. On Gandhi Jayanti, the answer to a call for protest in the capital has been to switch off the internet for everyone who lives, works, trades and reports in its centre. We call for the immediate restoration of services. 

At the time of release of this statement, we have not been able to locate any suspension order published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. The public does not know who directed this shutdown, on what grounds, over what area, or until when. IFF is attempting to trace the order and will make it public as soon as we obtain a copy.

In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that speech and trade over the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, and that every suspension order must be published, reasoned, proportionate and limited in time. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, only the Union or State Home Secretary may issue such an order, for reasons recorded in writing. The order must be published and must specify the area, the services and a fixed duration and it may be passed only where no other reasonable means would serve. A shutdown announced to subscribers as lasting "till further notice", imposed before a single person had assembled, cannot be squared with these safeguards. It follows repeated suspensions around Jantar Mantar in July 2026. Switching off the network is becoming a routine response to protest in the national capital. IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. 

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore mobile internet services in Connaught Place and all affected parts of Central Delhi.

2. Publish the suspension order forthwith, together with the reasons recorded in writing.

3. Disclose the issuing authority, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation.

4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days, as the Rules require, and make its findings public.

WHEN MAINSTREAM MEDIA FAILS TO SHOW THE PROTEST, CITIZENS WILL DOCUMENT IT THEMSELVES

The clip argues that sections of what it calls “Godi media” attempted to minimise or avoid showing the ongoing protests, while the demonstrations were nevertheless receiving widespread circulation through social media and other channels. 

Whatever one’s political position, the underlying democratic principle is important: no media ecosystem should become the sole gatekeeper of what citizens are allowed to see.

The current protests over the Election Commission and electoral-roll revision have received substantial coverage from multiple independent and mainstream outlets. Reports today confirm continuing INDIA-bloc demonstrations, attempts to reach Jantar Mantar, police detentions, and competing claims about the conduct of the protests. The Election Commission and BJP have rejected the allegations concerning electoral manipulation. 

That makes the responsibility of journalism even greater:

SHOW THE PROTEST.
SHOW THE POLICE RESPONSE.
SHOW THE GOVERNMENT'S POSITION.
SHOW THE ELECTION COMMISSION'S RESPONSE.
SHOW THE EVIDENCE.
AND LET CITIZENS DECIDE.

Criticism of media organisations is legitimate. But the resistance must not replace one form of information control with another.

Independent journalism, citizen journalism and social media should complement one another—not become competing propaganda machines.

The democratic test is simple:

Can citizens see the same events from multiple sources, examine the evidence and reach their own conclusions?

If yes, democracy is strengthened.

If inconvenient events are hidden, distorted or selectively presented, public trust suffers.

NO BLIND FAITH IN GOVERNMENT.
NO BLIND FAITH IN OPPOSITION.
NO BLIND FAITH IN MEDIA.
NO BLIND FAITH IN SOCIAL MEDIA.

LISTEN. VERIFY. COMPARE. THINK.
THEN SPEAK.

That is the kind of informed citizenry that makes democratic resistance durable.
